newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil output rebound will be slow in coming.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil output rebound will be slow in coming.

text.p: A major recovery in Russian oil production is still some years away, because Russia's new energy majors have neither the money nor the export outlets needed to boost output significantly, energy analysts said on Tuesday.

High tax burdens, low domestic oil prices, limited export capacity and outdated infrastructure are all helping to keep a lid on Russian output, which fell to 293 million tonnes (5.86 million barrels per day) in 1996, the lowest in nearly 30 years.

"I think we have basically reached the bottom of the cycle," said Stephen O'Sullivan, director of oil and gas at MC Securities in London, referring to a decade-long decline that has halved output from its peak 1987 level.
"But there will not be a recovery in the same shape as we saw in the decline."
A string of recent Russian oil company results supports the view that any rebound in production will be slow at best, and many small and medium-sized producers expect a slight output drop in 1997.
Russia's total oil output drop of two percent in 1996 was an improvement on 1995 in that it was the smallest drop in years.
But it still told a story of a persistant downward production trend in Russia, the world's third-largest oil producer.
"Realistically, companies could expect in coming years to boost output overall by three to four percent, but anything beyond that would be tough," said a Western oil consultant.
LUKoil, Russia's largest oil producer, saw 1996 output rise to 58.3 million tonnes from 57.3 million and forecast it edging up to 59.7 million this year.
But YUKOS, a top-three Russian producer, forecasts 1997 output down seven percent to 32.6 million.
Analysts said a January government decision to reduce excise duties on domestic output for most oil firms was a step in the right direction.
The changes are expected to cut the average duty to 55,000 roubles per tonne of oil from 72,000 roubles, according to a Renaissance Capital report.
Still, there is precious little cash to invest in boosting output significantly, in spite of a nine percent surge in Russian oil exports to pricier world markets last year.

"In some cases they (Russian oil companies) are saying that 80 percent of revenue is taken up by taxes, which doesn't leave much capital to reinvest in restructuring," said James Bunch, oil analyst at Renaissance Capital in Moscow.
Many oil firms are likely to concentrate first on improving production at existing facilities, rather than embarking on larger-scale developments.
"Virgin fields are incredibly costly to develop because of their location," said one senior Western oil analyst, referring to the high cost of developing huge mineral reserves in Siberia.
Russian oil output will only really take off when big development projects, many of which are stalled production-sharing deals with Western companies, get off the ground.
But progress has been slow, with political opposition to the deals strong in the State Duma lower parliament house.
"The mega-projects are just not moving ahead. By this I mean Sakhalin, Priobsk and Timan-Pechora," O'Sullivan said, referring to giant production-sharing deals with Western majors.
"In the short-term they should aim at operating existing infrastructure better, bringing idle wells back into production and getting existing wells to produce more."
Significant increases in oil output also depend on improving and widening export outlets.

With domestic consumption slow to recover from the slump in recent years, oil producers would have to ship any extra barrels abroad. But Russia's ageing export system is already creaking under the pressure of last year's export volumes.
"The question is whether there is a (domestic) market for more oil," Bunch said. "Russia is still not hungry for it."
